The collapse occurred just after 4 p.m. Eastern time Wednesday at a three-story building on Flatbush Avenue near Bedford Avenue in Flatbush.The New York City Police Department said a building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. was completely collapsed, while the side of an adjacent building at 1323 Flatbush Ave. was torn off in the process.According to police, the building that fully collapsed was occupied by residents at the time. Photos and video from the scene showed the exposed interiors of stairwells and apartments in the neighboring building. The cause of the collapse is under investigation. The site next to those two buildings was vacant and under construction, and multiple people from both the collapsed building and the construction site were trapped, officials said.More than 250 firefighters and EMS personnel responded to the site. New York City Fire Department Chief of Department John Esposito said a fire company that was in the neighborhood arrived on the scene less than one minute after the collapse."They encountered people trapped in the adjacent building that was part of the collapse. They immediately took action and removed those people from danger," Esposito said.Five people were killed and at least 19 others were injured, including seven children, officials said. FDNY officials said that of the injured, four people were in critical condition and 15 were in stable condition, including one firefighter with minor injuries.Officials have not yet released the ages of the victims who were killed.FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said investigators do not know how many people may still be in the collapse zone or how many people are missing."We know that we're not finished here, and we will likely not be finished for quite some time," Bonsignore said."We will be here for several days until this entire site is searched for all potential victims," Esposito said.Anyone who is unable to reach someone who may have been affected by the collapse is urged to call 311, or 212-639-9675 if you are outside New York City.Firefighters could be seen sifting through the rubble by hand and breaking through a collapsed wall to search underneath it. national.title: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in wilderness: "Grounded for life"
national.summary: Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed the boy was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.
national.body: A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands. The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 185 kilometers (115 miles) east of Melbourne, police said. A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said. Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets. "I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son. "And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.Police video showed Elizabeth embrace her son after the rescue helicopter landed to complete its mission. William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said."Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health," they said in the statement.William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360. Such a person may have marked deficits in verbal and non-verbal social communication and rely heavily on routines and predictable activities. Disruption can cause significant distress. The Southern Hemisphere spring weather had been mild for the past week in the alpine region where William was lost and there had been little rain. Elizabeth had dropped off her son and his friend last Friday for a weekend of camping. William walked a short distance from the campsite to the drop-off location to collect more camping equipment but never returned to his friend, police said. After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down "some very steep terrain," Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said. He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surrounds 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the his camp site, Benbow said. national.title: New York building collapse kills at least four people
national.summary: A dangerous search for survivors continues after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday afternoon.
national.body:
At least four people have died after a building in New York City collapsed into an open construction site on Wednesday afternoon.

Nineteen others have been injured, of whom four are in a critical condition, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News, which cited local officials.

The collapse sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders going to the scene of the fallen three-storey building in Brooklyn.

Aerial footage has shown firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher. She was later said to have been a pregnant woman.

Officials previously said they did not know how many others are missing. The BBC has contacted the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) for further comment.

An investigation is under way into what caused the sudden collapse.

Witnesses described a terrifying sound as the building came down at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT).

"I live literally right behind the building," one woman, Emmanuella Carilus, told the New York Times. "It sounded like a big boom and you just heard a bunch of screaming."

national.summary: President Trump spoke about the Iran war during a Veterans Day address at Arlington National Cemetery.
national.body: The head of Iran's feared paramilitary police force the Basij said Thursday that Iran would "decide on the manner and agenda of any negotiations only after its seven conditions are fulfilled and accepted by the other side," according to Iranian state news agency IRNA. It was a reiteration of Iran's refusal to budge on its core demands for a preliminary peace deal with the U.S. — and a seemingly deliberate response to President Trump's assertion on Wednesday that the costly conflict had already been a victory for his administration, and it was "just a question of when we want to end it." Basij chief Hossein Taeb said it made no difference to Iran how long the process of ending the war might take, and that "the main issue is the fulfillment of the conditions set by the Islamic Republic of Iran. After that, Iran will decide on the manner and subjects of negotiations." As laid out by Vahid Ahmadi, a member of the Iranian Parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission at the end of September, the conditions that must be met before "substantive negotiations" on matters such as Iran's nuclear program can begin are: An ending to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon and Gaza The easing of what Iran considers "unjust and illegal sanctions" The lifting of the U.S. naval blockade of Iran's ports and vessels An accepted system for Iran and Oman to control Strait of Hormuz traffic A plan to compensate Iran for damage inflicted during the war The release of frozen Iranian financial assets held abroad An end to all threats against Iran "These issues only make sense when considered together," Vahid said at the time, adding that some of the conditions could potentially be met during an initial ceasefire, rather than as a prerequisite for one. "You cannot continue threats and war on the one hand, maintain maritime restrictions, keep Iran's assets frozen and refuse to compensate for the damage inflicted, while expecting Iran to enter serious negotiations on the other," he said, according to the Iranian news outlet IRAF. Speaking Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Iran's demands "unacceptable" and made it clear there was little expectation of any near-term diplomatic breakthrough. national.title: Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
national.summary: The guard told the defence secretary and his companions to maintain an atmosphere of "silence and respect" during a Veterans Day visit.
national.body:
The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

national.title: ICE deportations and arrests hit record high
national.summary: New Department of Homeland Security figures show more than 483,000 deportations and 491,000 immigration arrests in fiscal year 2026.
national.body: Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported a record 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, according to new Department of Homeland Security figures obtained by CBS News, marking a historic escalation in President Trump's signature immigration crackdown, even as voters grapple with the increase in interior enforcement. The total number of individuals deported represents the highest annual figure in ICE's reported history, surpassing the law enforcement agency's previous record of 442,640 in fiscal year 2025. ICE also reported more than 491,000 immigration arrests during the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests — another record, according to DHS. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges. The records underscore a defining feature of Mr. Trump's second presidency — a sweeping enforcement campaign reshaped by dramatic immigration policy and the operational expansion of the federal law enforcement footprint in communities far from the border. But they also arrive at a politically complicated moment for Mr. Trump. Following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections, the president has publicly acknowledged that parts of his deportation campaign may have gone too far. Yet that admission was coupled with a decision to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his most restrictive immigration policies, to White House chief of staff. These new figures underscore a tension further reflected within American public opinion. CBS News polls have shown widespread support for border security alongside increasing discomfort with how immigration laws are enforced in communities nationwide. Behind the record-breaking numbers According to DHS, the new deportation total is approximately 18% higher than the 409,849 removals ICE recorded in fiscal year 2012, during the Obama administration, a longstanding agency benchmark. The new record is also nearly 78% higher than the 271,484 deportations recorded in fiscal year 2024, the last full fiscal year under President Biden.ICE reported a total of 50,925 arrests in the month of August alone, eclipsing the previous monthly high set in July. national.summary: Republicans described the incoming minority leader as a "fighter" who can go head to head with Hakeem Jeffries.
national.body: Washington — Former House Speaker John Boehner once described Rep. Jim Jordan, the next House Republican leader, as a political "terrorist." "I just never saw a guy who spent more time tearing things apart, never building anything, never putting anything together," the former GOP leader told CBS News in 2021. On Tuesday, House Republicans selected Jordan to lead the party in the next Congress, a significant shakeup in the party's leadership that signaled they're ready for a fight after losing more than 40 seats in the midterm elections. Jordan — who was a founding member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, which routinely makes legislating difficult for GOP leaders — built his reputation confronting Democrats in combative hearings as the top Republican on the powerful House Judiciary Committee. There, the Ohio Republican defended President Trump against the first impeachment inquiry, which centered on the president's conduct toward Ukraine. "Jim's a fighter," said GOP Rep. Nicole Malliotakis of New York, who sees Jordan, a former college wrestling coach, as someone who can unite the various factions in the party. "I think a lot of the reasons why we couldn't get more done this Congress was because we could not unite the team. I think Jim Jordan is somebody who everybody respects and can bring everyone together." GOP Rep. Ralph Norman of South Carolina, who is retiring after losing a Senate primary, said Jordan represents "the side of the party that's willing to fight." Norman suggested that the conference chose Jordan over current Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana for the role because he "represented more of what they wanted to see as a minority leader." "There's nobody that can debate any better. There's nobody that can fight any more," Norman said. Republican Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland, the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, called Jordan a "superb communicator" who can go up against Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is expected to become House speaker in January. national.body: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported. And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall. Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. national.title: British woman missing from cruise ship in Atlantic
national.summary: The 72-year-old was last seen aboard the Tui ship on Monday as it headed towards the Caribbean.
national.body:
A British woman has gone missing from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic, travel operator Tui has said.

The 72-year-old was last seen aboard Tui's Marella Voyager on Monday while the vessel was en route to the Caribbean. The ship could have travelled hundreds of miles in the time between when she was last seen to when she was reported missing.

Staff realised the passenger was missing on Tuesday, when they noticed her bed had not been slept in. The alarm was raised and a search carried out, Tui said in a statement.

It is understood the missing guest was then reported to the US Coast Guard, which asked the ship to continue to its crossing rather than reverse course and search for the woman.

Holidaymakers were told to abandon dinners, drinks and entertainment as the crew carried out an emergency headcount on Tuesday evening, the Daily Mail reports.

Passengers stood in lines of four while staff scanned boarding cards to verify the identity of every person on the ship, according to the newspaper.

The USCG Rescue Co-ordination Centre in Norfolk, Virginia has issued an alert calling on any ships nearby to "keep a sharp look out" for the woman, the Mail reports. The BBC has contacted the USCG for comment.

The Marella Voyager, carrying around 2,000 passengers and 800 crew, left Malaga on 4 November and is due to arrive in Antigua on Friday before calling at Dominica and finishing its voyage in Barbados on Sunday.

national.title: US envoys arrive in Moscow for Ukraine talks with Vladimir Putin
national.summary: Later on Thursday, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will travel to Dublin to meet Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
national.body:
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Videos shared by Russian media showed Kushner and Witkoff disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.

The American negotiatiors were due to meet Putin at 12:00 local time (09:00 GMT), and will then fly to Dublin to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

On Tuesday, Kushner said the US had seen "some openings and some opportunities" and that they would try to "make some progress" at the meeting with Putin.

The in-person talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents were only announced on Wednesday after two days of talks which were framed as centred around the postwar security architecture of Europe.

Nearly five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow shows no sign of backing down from its maximalist demands for sovereign Ukrainian territory and for Western countries to give up any future commitment to protecting Kyiv in case of further attacks.

During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.

However, in recent times many have grown concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin, and have been pushing for a seat at the negotiating table.

national.title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
national.summary: In a state Trump won two years ago by 22 points, Colom's victory extends a string of Democratic wins in the Senate.
national.body:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.

Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.

national.title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from district attorney to Mississippi's Democratic US Senator
national.summary: In a state that hasn't had a Democrat in office since 1980 and hasn't sent a Black Senator to Washington since the 1870s, Colom's win represents a massive upset in state politics.
national.body:
JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.

But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.

"We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend – we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."

Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.

Colom won by less than five thousand votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.

While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote.

Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County – an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base .

Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.

national.title: At least 23 states considered laws governing ICE and schools this year
national.summary: When ICE agents show up at a school, educators rely on a patchwork of policies to know what to do. This year, many state legislatures tried to update those policies.
national.body:
Andrea Garza says it's not unusual or alarming when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are spotted near a school in Laredo, Texas, a border town.

In other parts of the country, "seeing the presence of border patrol would be, you know, different, maybe shocking. Just something from another world, right?" she said. "It's something very normal here."

Garza is a school leader with the United Independent School District , which serves Laredo. Federal data shows 94% of her district's community is Hispanic. Garza said some families have been in Laredo for generations, while others came more recently, and the federal government is one of her area's largest employers.

She said she knows what she would do if ICE comes knocking: If they don't have a warrant or subpoena, they don't get in.

"We serve 'in loco parentis' for students," she said, meaning "in place of a parent" when the students' rights are challenged.

"It's not interpreted, in the way we see it, as interfering with the law," Garza explained. "It is more just verifying that we are all following the law."

Texas state law prohibits local entities, including campus police, from obstructing federal immigration enforcement. But NPR found no state laws that directly address how much access these officers should have in K-12 public schools.

Only on NPR Why public schools nationwide are facing a massive drop in student enrollment And it's not just Texas. Many states lack clear policies governing what these interactions should look like. Recent federal changes haven't helped.

national.title: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
national.summary: A Supreme Court ruling that further weakened the Voting Rights Act paved the way for a record drop in Black representation in Congress. But a midterm blue wave helped hold off such a decline for now.
national.body:
Democratic Reps. Terri Sewell (left) and Shomari Figures of Alabama appear at a voting rights rally in May on the steps of the state's Capitol in Montgomery, Ala. Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect hide caption

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that further weakened the Voting Rights Act raised the possibility of a record drop in Black representation in Congress.

But a Democratic blue wave in the midterm elections helped forestall such a decline for now.

Most notably, Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, won reelection despite Alabama's Republican state leaders making his district far more GOP-leaning after the court's decision.

Only on NPR The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decline next year, according to an NPR analysis. The incoming Congress is set to include 60 Black House members, including nonvoting members, down from 63 in the current House. That's just one away from the record loss of four Black representatives after the 1876 election, around the end of the Reconstruction era.

In addition to the unprecedented mid-decade redistricting fight, the usual churn of politics, including members retiring or running for higher office , contributed to next year's falling tally.

But high Black voter turnout, especially in the South , fueled Democratic wins that have offset the upcoming decline in the number of Black members of the House.

Voting rights advocates and redistricting experts warn, however, that the redrawing of district lines in the coming years, including after the 2030 census , continues to pose a threat to Black representation in Congress.

national.title: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say
national.summary: The text of what lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. A group of open governance advocates is calling on Senate leadership for a change.
national.body:
If you want to know what bills are under consideration in the Senate, you could follow floor proceedings live on C-SPAN. But, even for parliamentary procedure experts, it can be difficult to understand exactly what's happening.

Among the issues? The text of what the lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. Now, a crosspartisan group of open governance advocates has sent a letter to Senate leadership calling for change. In the letter, first obtained by NPR, they call on the Senate to post bill and amendment text online as soon as it is made available to members.

"The public and the press and the whole apparatus that supports the Senate to help understand what legislation is, they don't have access," said Daniel Schuman, an author on the letter and the executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to strengthening the institutions of American democracy.

Congress House GOP elects Jim Jordan as new leader as the party looks to rebuild from midterms That lack of transparency means "that problems can often sneak through," said Schuman. "At times, this has been a mechanism for the Senate to move legislation to avoid the proper public scrutiny." In 2013, Schuman recalled, Congress quietly repealed provisions of a popular congressional financial disclosure and insider trading law — skirting public scrutiny.

While the Congressional Record — the official record of legislative branch proceedings and debates — does provide information about bill text and proposed amendments, it is not published until after the legislative day concludes. That means when bills or amendments are offered on the same day they are considered, they may not be publicly available until after they are voted on.

national.title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from district attorney to Mississippi's Democratic US Senator
national.summary: In a state that hasn't had a Democrat in office since 1980 and hasn't sent a Black Senator to Washington since the 1870s, Colom's win represents a massive upset in state politics.
national.body:
JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.

But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.

"We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend – we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."

Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.

Colom won by less than five thousand votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.

While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote.

Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County – an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base .

Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.

national.summary: A Supreme Court ruling that further weakened the Voting Rights Act paved the way for a record drop in Black representation in Congress. But a midterm blue wave helped hold off such a decline for now.
national.body:
Democratic Reps. Terri Sewell (left) and Shomari Figures of Alabama appear at a voting rights rally in May on the steps of the state's Capitol in Montgomery, Ala. Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect hide caption

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that further weakened the Voting Rights Act raised the possibility of a record drop in Black representation in Congress.

But a Democratic blue wave in the midterm elections helped forestall such a decline for now.

Most notably, Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, won reelection despite Alabama's Republican state leaders making his district far more GOP-leaning after the court's decision.

Only on NPR The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decline next year, according to an NPR analysis. The incoming Congress is set to include 60 Black House members, including nonvoting members, down from 63 in the current House. That's just one away from the record loss of four Black representatives after the 1876 election, around the end of the Reconstruction era.

In addition to the unprecedented mid-decade redistricting fight, the usual churn of politics, including members retiring or running for higher office , contributed to next year's falling tally.

But high Black voter turnout, especially in the South , fueled Democratic wins that have offset the upcoming decline in the number of Black members of the House.

Voting rights advocates and redistricting experts warn, however, that the redrawing of district lines in the coming years, including after the 2030 census , continues to pose a threat to Black representation in Congress.

national.title: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say
national.summary: The text of what lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. A group of open governance advocates is calling on Senate leadership for a change.
national.body:
If you want to know what bills are under consideration in the Senate, you could follow floor proceedings live on C-SPAN. But, even for parliamentary procedure experts, it can be difficult to understand exactly what's happening.

Among the issues? The text of what the lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. Now, a crosspartisan group of open governance advocates has sent a letter to Senate leadership calling for change. In the letter, first obtained by NPR, they call on the Senate to post bill and amendment text online as soon as it is made available to members.

"The public and the press and the whole apparatus that supports the Senate to help understand what legislation is, they don't have access," said Daniel Schuman, an author on the letter and the executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to strengthening the institutions of American democracy.

"At times, this has been a mechanism for the Senate to move legislation to avoid the proper public scrutiny." In 2013, Schuman recalled, Congress quietly repealed provisions of a popular congressional financial disclosure and insider trading law — skirting public scrutiny.

While the Congressional Record — the official record of legislative branch proceedings and debates — does provide information about bill text and proposed amendments, it is not published until after the legislative day concludes. That means when bills or amendments are offered on the same day they are considered, they may not be publicly available until after they are voted on.

national.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
national.summary: Witnesses say a missile hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units at Nasser hospital, the largest in southern Gaza.
national.body:
At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired by a warplane hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units overnight.

The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.

Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".

Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.

Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.

Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.

national.title: Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, health authorities say
national.summary: The victims included a surgeon, and dozens more were injured. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
national.body:
Medical staff inspect damage to Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip on Thursday. Abdel Kareem Hana/AP hide caption

KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip — An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a general surgeon, and wounded at least 28 more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.

The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence.

The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgical wing and that a doctor, Rizk Abu Shaira, was among the dead. Inside the building, parts of several floors were either severely damaged or destroyed. Debris was scattered across hospital beds and equipment, and rebar dangled from the ceiling where the munition had penetrated.

British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.

"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department when the bomb hit. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.

He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," he said.

Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war.

national.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for President Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
national.body:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government.

Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid.

His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto.

Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president.

"[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia".

"He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

national.title: 'No light, no water, no heat': Ukrainians struggle with blackouts as Russia hits power grid
national.summary: For parents in parts of Ukraine, trying to lead a normal family life with just a few hours of power each day is taking its toll.
national.body:
Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."

As peace talks continue, with US envoys meeting the Russian and Ukrainian leaders on Thursday, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.

Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.

The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.

The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.

According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.

Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.

Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.

A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.

Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.

national.summary: For Nigerians to feel meaningful improvements, reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined, analysts say.
national.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.

The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.

Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.

Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.

The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.

The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.

national.body:
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures could be ousted from his role amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.

Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.

Now the firm is reportedly weighing whether to remove Huang after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.

Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.

Nvidia's board was reportedly meeting on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.

Nvidia has 11 directors on its board, including Huang, and the CEO can be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors, according to Reuters news agency.

Should Nvidia's board choose to oust Huang, or place him on leave, it was not immediately clear who might step into his shoes, even on an interim basis.

national.title: Famed ship SS United States deliberately sunk off Florida coast to become a reef
national.summary: Activists wanted the historic liner to be turned into a museum, but it will instead become the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
national.body:
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic has intentionally been sunk off the coast of Florida, turning into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.

Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it was added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, with a land-based museum detailing the ship's history also planned.

Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities between the US and Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.

A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work.

On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it was sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.

national.summary: The 1,000-foot-long SS United States was sent to the bottom of the ocean in a controlled, explosive-free sinking that is taking place about 20 nautical miles off the Gulf Coast of Florida.
national.body: The SS United States, the fabled ocean liner, was scuttled toward the ocean floor on Wednesday in a controlled, explosive-free sinking that took place about 20 nautical miles off the Gulf Coast of Florida between the Destin-Fort Walton Beach region and Pensacola. The 1,000-foot-long SS United States was sent to the bottom of the ocean in an hourslong sinking operation that began Wednesday afternoon and concluded later in the evening. The ship will become the world's largest artificial reef, only adding to its long list of maritime achievements. The Destin-Fort Walton Beach metropolitan area says it already has about 580 artificial reefs off its coastline, the most for any region in the country. The SS United States first set sail in 1952, at the time setting a transatlantic speed record for an ocean liner that still stands today.It carried thousands of voyagers over its two decades of military service, including presidents, royalty, celebrities and even legendary CBS News broadcaster Walter Cronkite. Its design was so revolutionary that even the Pentagon kept it a secret.But by 1969, the SS United States was retired from service, and it wound up in Philadelphia in 1996. It remained docked there for decades, until Okaloosa County in Florida purchased the ship from the SS United States Conservancy for about $1 million in 2024 with the goal of deploying it as an artificial reef designed to provide a habitat for the Gulf's marine ecosystem. Prior to sinking it, the county sent the ship to Mobile, Alabama, for a one-year preparation process that involved removing all environmentally unsafe materials, including non-metal items, wiring and fuel, the county said. Holes were also strategically cut throughout the ship to ensure it remains upright when submerged. The preparations were conducted in coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The approximately $13 million project to make the ship an artificial reef was funded by county tourist tax revenue. Okaloosa County hopes that the ship will serve as a jolt to the economy of the Florida Panhandle, providing a year-round destination for divers. "I think it's going to be like Disney World," Jocelyn Collins, general manager for Emerald Coast Scuba, told CBS News. "You know, we're going to line people up and take pictures underwater."

national.summary: The SS United States broke trans-Atlantic speed records. On Wednesday, it was sunk off the Florida coast and will become a diving destination and home for marine life.
national.body:
The SS United States, without its smokestacks, at port in Mobile, Ala., before its sinking on Wednesday. Destin-Fort Walton Beach/Screenshot by NPR hide caption

The fastest passenger liner in the world crossed the Atlantic Ocean in less than four days. On Wednesday, it sank in five hours.

National SS United States, record-setting ocean liner, makes its final voyage The SS United States, launched in 1951 and longer than the RMS Titanic, once transported four presidents, the Mona Lisa and a slate of 20th century movie stars. After decades spent rusting , and facing the scrap heap, its minders settled on a deal to turn the vessel into what's expected to be the world's largest artificial reef off the coast of Okaloosa County, Fla.

Crews removed plugs in the ship's hull, allowing it to fill with water without the use of explosives. After hours of delays, its final moments went quickly. The ship tilted onto its side and dipped below the waves.

The sinking marks a bittersweet coda to the era of gleaming behemoths that crossed the seas in elegant fashion. It is also the latest in an ongoing effort by coastal communities to lure thrill-seeking tourists away from international destinations, one that has so far generated surprising economic benefits.

"For those of us who love shipwrecks and love ships in general, it was way more tragic to see it sitting and rusting away at the dock," wreck diver and maritime enthusiast Karen Flynn told NPR.

Her diving club, the Maryland-based Atlantic Wreck Divers, booked tickets and a charter boat just days after a date for the ship's "deployment," as the sinking is diplomatically described, was set.

"We've dove everything that you can around the world," Flynn said. "This will just be one more unique, new thing for us to dive."

national.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
national.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".
national.body:
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.

William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.

Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.

He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".

Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.

The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.

"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.

"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."

national.title: Hegseth's group reprimanded for noise at Tomb of Unknown Soldier
national.summary: A guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanded a group of people that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for making noise at the site.
national.body: Washington — A guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday loudly reprimanded a group of people that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for making noise at the site.Hegseth, his wife and several aides — including chief of staff Ricky Buria — visited the tomb for a Veterans Day wreath-laying, followed by a ceremony at the nearby Memorial Auditorium. President Trump and first lady Melania Trump also attended the event. After the ceremony, the defense secretary and his team posed for a photo. As they began walking away, a member of the group audibly laughed, leading a U.S. Army sentinel to belt out: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."It is not clear who laughed, or whether Hegseth made any noise.Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."CNN was first to report on the incident.The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier memorializes deceased American service members from World War I and later conflicts whose remains were never identified. The sentinels who march in front of the tomb for 24 hours a day — a prestigious posting within the Army — are a well-known presence at the cemetery, famous for their guard-changing ceremony.It is not unusual for sentinels to reprimand visitors who interrupt the solemnity expected at the memorial. Army Staff Sgt. Chadwick Winget, who belonged to the regiment that guards the tomb, said in a 2022 Army interview that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

local.title: PBS documentary series "Crime and Punishment" features the story of Rochester's Austin Reed
local.summary: Reed was born into Rochester's free Black community in 1823 and was later incarcerated. His memoir describes violence and torture behind bars.
local.body:
A new PBS documentary series premiering Monday, Nov. 16 on WXXI-TV features the story of a Rochester native.

"Crime and Punishment in America" is a four-part series examining criminal justice in America from the colonial era to today.

Austin Reed was a Black man who was born free in Rochester in 1823. But his freedom would not last long. After his father died when he was a young child, Reed became an indentured servant and was later sent to the House of Refuge in New York City.

"Which was essentially a prison for children with a bit of schooling," said Lynn Novick, producer and director of the film series.

Reed eventually returned to Rochester and was in and out of prison for 20 years.

His memoir, "The Adventures of a Haunted Convict," documents his experiences with violence and torture as an incarcerated person in his youth and at Auburn Prison in upstate New York.

"He's really wrestling with what is prison for? Why are we torturing people? How do we reckon with the things we've done wrong in this moment and in these kind of places?" Novick said.

local.title: Rochester School for the Deaf alumna debuts first book, 'Siren of the Finger Lakes'
local.summary: The glacially-formed landscape of the Finger Lakes is the home of Kristen Sickler's creation, "The Siren of the Finger Lakes," which is now a book — and her first publication under her imprint, The Siren Current Press.
local.body:
Listen • 1:13 The 11 Finger Lakes have a magnetic pull for deaf author Kristen Sickler.

The glacially-formed landscape is the home of her creation, "The Siren of the Finger Lakes," which is now a book — and her first publication under her imprint, The Siren Current Press.

The story is family-friendly and narrated by 9-year-old Liv, a girl who grows up in the Finger Lakes region and pieces together what it is about this place that holds so much meaning within the land and the waters.

Sickler grew up in the area, graduated from the Rochester School for the Deaf, and now lives in Avon. She said the idea came to her last year on Sept. 30, her birthday and the anniversary of her mother's death nine years before. The book was published exactly one year later.

"There's something about all of that coming together on the same date that I hold incredibly close to my heart," Sicklerwrote in an email. " I genuinely believe my mother has been part of this journey in her own way."

Sickler said she has always loved the mysterious and unknown. But while this story touches those themes, she said it felt familiar from the moment she envisioned it.

"I'm surprised that the story hadn't already been thought of before," Sickler said in American Sign Language, speaking through an interpreter. "I'm like, 'How could I possibly be the first one who could concoct something like this?' It's almost strange."

The book is just 40 pages, accounting for short attention spans, Sickler said, while giving readers a sense of connection to a region that carries special meaning to her.

local.title: Groundbreaking for High Falls State Park to take place next week
local.summary: The first phase of the park will break ground Wednesday, and will focus on the Heritage Walk on the eastern rim of High Falls gorge.
local.body:
The groundbreaking for the first phase of High Falls State Park will take place Wednesday, Nov. 18, officials have confirmed.

The first phase of park construction will be High Falls Terrace, overlooking the eastern edge of the gorge. The core of that project phase is the Heritage Walk and Memorial Wall, dedicated to the stories of those who migrated to the Rochester area, from Irish Americans to the Haudenosaunee nations.

Two public hearings hosted by the state later this month will examine the potential environmental impact of the park. The New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation then will prepare a report that details "potentially significant adverse environmental impacts and reasonable alternatives to be evaluated, and outlines the studies and analyses anticipated to support environmental review."

The planned 85-acre park encompassing the High Falls Gorge would be the first state park in the city of Rochester. Its construction would include the development of about five miles of paved pathways, as well as six overlooks, restrooms, and an assortment of pavilions, playgrounds and other amenities.

Local News From the archive: See the designs for High Falls State Park Brian Sharp “A centerpiece of the updated design is the new Heritage Walk, which will be a memorial centered on immigration and the migration of people to Rochester,” according to a release detailing the first phase. Erik Frisch is commissioner of the city's Department of Neighborhood and Business Development. He said the park will likely be a major draw to a part of the city that formerly only served industrial purposes.

"If other urban state park examples are proof of concept, then you know we can expect hundreds of thousands of new visitors coming into the city, into High Falls, to experience this state park, and literally to experience something that has not been experienced prior to the creation of the park," Frisch said.

Public comments on the project will be given in virtual webinars, set for 6 p.m. Nov. 19 and 11 a.m. Nov. 20. Written comments will be accepted through Dec. 6.

The state's parks department declined an interview for this story, instead offering a written statement. In the statement provided to WXXI News, the process was described as standard protocol for projects like High Falls State Park. The final document is meant to guide the project on "potentially significant adverse environmental impacts," "provide an initial identification of mitigation measures," and "provide the public with an opportunity to participate in the identification of impacts," among other goals.

local.title: CWD found in a Sparta deer
local.summary: New York’s big game hunting season has long offered more than the excitement of pursuing whitetails. For thousands of hunters, it represents an opportunity to put healthy, locally harvested venison in the freezer, helping supplement grocery bills while carrying on a deeply rooted outdoor tradition.
local.body:
New York’s big game hunting season has long offered more than the excitement of pursuing whitetails. For thousands of hunters, it represents an opportunity to put healthy, locally harvested venison in the freezer, helping supplement grocery bills while carrying on a deeply rooted outdoor tradition. One of New York’s biggest selling points for hunters, including those traveling hundreds of miles from other states and Canada, has been its long-standing success in keeping Chronic Wasting Disease out of the wild deer population.

The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation recently confirmed CWD in a wild white-tailed deer harvested in the town of Sparta, Livingston County. It marks the first detection in a wild deer in New York since 2005 and has prompted DEC to activate its CWD Response Plan to determine how widespread the disease may be and take steps to prevent further spread.

The news is certainly concerning, but it is also an opportunity to recognize the tremendous effort that has gone into protecting New York’s deer herd over the past two decades.

CWD first appeared in New York in 2005, when the disease was discovered in captive deer facilities in Oneida County. Subsequent testing identified two infected wild deer nearby. DEC, working with the Department of Agriculture and Markets, launched an intensive response involving testing, containment, and the removal of affected deer. The effort ultimately eliminated that outbreak, making New York a notable success story in CWD management. Since then, tens of thousands of deer have been tested through ongoing surveillance without another positive wild-deer detection until now.

That vigilance matters. In 2025 alone, DEC tested more than 3,000 deer for CWD as part of its statewide monitoring program. Although a captive deer herd in Herkimer County tested positive in 2024, targeted testing did not identify the disease in surrounding wild deer. The Livingston County finding remains the only newly identified positive wild-deer detection in the state.

CWD is a highly contagious, always-fatal disease affecting the brain and nervous system of deer, elk, and moose. While there is no evidence that it can infect humans or domestic livestock, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends against consuming venison from an animal known to have CWD.

For hunters in the newly established containment area, which includes Conesus, Groveland, North Dansville, Sparta, Springwater and West Sparta, additional precautions are now required. All harvested deer must be submitted for tissue sampling, and whole deer cannot be transported outside the containment area without following DEC’s transport requirements. Collection locations and instructions are available through DEC’s CWD information resources.

local.summary: Milwaukee’s Jacob Misiorowski and the New York Yankees’ Cam Schlittler were unanimous Cy Young Award winners Wednesday night after delivering dominant performances in their first full major league seasons. Misiorowski, who reached 105.5 mph with his fastball this summer, won the NL award after helpi
local.body:
Milwaukee’s Jacob Misiorowski and the New York Yankees’ Cam Schlittler were unanimous Cy Young Award winners Wednesday night after delivering dominant performances in their first full major league seasons.

Misiorowski, who reached 105.5 mph with his fastball this summer, won the NL award after helping the Brewers win their first World Series title. Schlittler became the second Yankees pitcher in four years to receive the AL award.

The right-handers made their major league debuts in the summer of 2025.

“It’s exciting,” Misiorowski said. “And then you look one year past that and you’ve got (2025 NL Cy Young Award winner) Paul Skenes also doing it in his second year. It’s really cool, the youth that’s coming up in the big leagues. It’s going to be fun to watch for years to come.”

This was the third time both Cy Young winners were unanimous picks by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Houston’s Justin Verlander won in the AL in 2022 and Miami’s Sandy Alcantara in the NL, and Detroit’s Denny McLain won in the AL in 1968 and St. Louis’ Bob Gibson in the NL.

“Realistically when you come into your first full season of the year, do you think you’re going to do that? Maybe not,” Schlittler said. “But you also have the confidence that you can do that. I definitely had conversations with guys in spring training, and that’s kind of a minor goal you put for yourself. I’m just glad to live up to the expectations.”

Misiorowski is 24 and Schlittler is 25, making this the fourth time that both Cy Young winners were 25 or younger, according to Sportradar. The other instances were in 1969 (Tom Seaver and McLain), 1985 (Dwight Gooden and Bret Saberhagen) and 2009 (Tim Lincecum and Zack Greinke).

Toronto’s Louis Varland won the BBWAA’s inaugural AL Reliever of the Year award, while San Diego’s Mason Miller was a unanimous selection for the NL version.

local.body:
Halloween 2026 is history, but the spooks are still standing on many front lawns. You know the ones - the 12-foot skeletons that tower over the rhododendrons - and make me anxious, even at this age. At least the bloody ghouls are mostly packed away now.

I never liked Halloween. I know, I know. It's almost unamerican. But it started early and never really went away. I was an outcast on Halloween.

As an only child, and the only girl in an all-boy neighborhood, I never had anyone to trick-or-treat with. The boys certainly didn't want to drag along that "sissy girl."

Back in the day, parents didn't go trick-or-treating with their costumed kids - they stayed home to answer the door and pass out homemade popcorn balls or candied apples. Full-sized candy bars were fairly common, and for a scaredy-cat like me they were the only reason to head out there alone. I was afraid of the dark streets, scared of the thick hedges, frightened of the shadows.

Mom's work schedule didn't allow time for sewing a costume, and store-bought costumes weren't big back then. The closest she came to actually making a custom costume for me was cutting up an old sheet to transform me into Casper the Friendly Ghost. A few days ahead of spook night, she surrendered an old sheet to the task.

I remember she dropped the middle of the sheet over my head to cut it to ankle length. "Hold still," she said, "I have to get this even all the way around." She felt for my nose bump so she could locate my eyes. "Don't move until I outline them both." Then she removed the sheet to cut out the eyeholes. "There, you're ready to scare everybody out of their best candy bars."

It wasn't easy keeping the crooked eyeholes lined up on Halloween night. I worked hard at not tripping up and down porch stairs and hanging on to my brown paper shopping bag. I wore "Casper" for three years. When the sheet was approaching knee length, it was time to retire the ghost. The next easiest costume? A witch, of course. And Mom was home that Halloween.

I was in the fourth or fifth grade when she jury-rigged the witch's hat for me. She had a pretty, large-brimmed black picture hat. With pieces of black construction paper, she fashioned a pointed cone that she pinned over the hat's crown. Adding an old black coat of hers that dragged on the ground after I was buttoned in, she declared me a wonderful witch. "But they can see my face," I complained. She then drew heavy dark circles around my eyes with her mascara. It was quite a transformation. I looked both scary and half dead - and not much like myself. I went out alone. Again. I always walked tense, fearful, and that year I struggled with the too-long coat, dragging it over the curbstones.

It’s been incredible,” said sophomore goalkeeper Angel Busch. “I don’t think anyone thought this was possible. Our goal was to
local.body:
JAMESTOWN -- It's already been a dream season for the Jamestown Community College women’s soccer team as they prepare for the NJCAA Division III Tournament.

"It's been crazy. It's been incredible," said sophomore goalkeeper Angel Busch. "I don't think anyone thought this was possible. Our goal was to win five games, and we've made it this far. It is pretty great."

The Jayhawks won their fifth game of the season Sept. 19 to improve to 5-0-0.

"I think a lot of us went into this season looking at it as a stepping stone year to eventually get here, but no one thought it would happen this quickly," said freshman midfielder Gracie Chimera.

Crazy, maybe. Historic for JCC, absolutely. The Jayhawks' 12 wins are a program record, and this squad is on pace to set a team-high for goals scored per game and the fewest goals allowed in a season. Most importantly, they're the first JCC women's soccer team to win a regional championship and advance to nationals.

"I think it is literally crazy," said sophomore forward Sarah Kruszka. "I don't have any other words for it. Seeing the banner in the gym, and it was empty, and now we're the first year to put it up there. That is something I'll tell my kids about. We did that."

"We have always joked that we will be the first team on the banner, and now we made it true," said freshman defender Kennady Ellsworth. "This has been one of my favorite years playing soccer ever."

All the accolades are deserved, but it begs the question: How did the Jayhawks flip the switch so quickly? The players point to their first-year head coach, Sarah Chimera, who brought together a collection of familiar talent she has known and coached for years throughout the Jamestown region.

But as the city begins paving over some of those historic roads, residents are weighing the loss of a familiar piece of their neighborhood against the need for safer, smoother streets.On Daisy Place, the change has been welcomed by residents who say the uneven bricks had become difficult to navigate, both for drivers and pedestrians.Ken Lee, who has lived on Daisy Place for about 25 years, said the condition of the road had become a problem for drivers."I think it is a beautiful thing because I have been on this street for about 25 years, and this street was terrible," Lee said. "Cars, you could hear them bottoming out when they go here. It was like having its own speed bump."Lee said drivers often had to maneuver around deep divots in the road."You would have to almost go on the sidewalk to escape the divots," he said.Billy Banks, who has also lived on Daisy Place for more than 20 years, shared photos showing the road's condition before it was paved. local.summary: The “street pricing” bill would limit what certain taxpayer-subsidized venues can charge for food and drinks. The effort comes as Bills fans face some of the NFL’s highest concession prices.
local.body: The cost of attending a Bills game is among the most expensive in the NFL, in large part due to the team's success on the field, which pushes up the price of tickets. But you'll also be digging deep into your pockets once you get through the gates.State lawmakers are scrutinizing the price of food and drinks inside Highmark Stadium and other venues that are subsidized by taxpayers.The issue was the focus of a hearing before the Assembly Committee on Consumer Affairs and Protection. Consumer advocates and other experts pushed for legislation that would limit some concession prices.Brian Hess, executive director of the nonprofit Sports Fans Coalition, testified at the hearing. He pointed to Highmark Stadium as an example of the problem, saying it sells the most expensive hot dog in the NFL at $11.63."Hot dogs don't cost $12," Hess said. "They cost the same to make in and out of the stadium, and fans should be given that flexibility and that choice."One proposal, Assembly Bill A8921, would require certain publicly subsidized sports and entertainment venues to follow what's known as "street pricing."Under the bill, concession prices for food and nonalcoholic beverages could be no more than 20% above the average price of comparable items at nearby businesses within a 10-mile radius.The proposal remains in committee and has not become law.Democratic Assemblymember Nily Rozic, chair of the Consumer Affairs and Protection Committee, described street pricing as a way to ensure consumers can buy everyday goods and refreshments at prices reasonably comparable to what they would pay outside a venue.Hess said he sensed bipartisan interest in addressing the issue during the hearing."I got that sense from the hearing loud and clear," he said.Some stadiums have already adopted lower concession prices voluntarily.At Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, home of the Falcons, the team introduced its "Fan First" pricing program. Cheeseburgers and domestic draft beer are among the items priced at $5.Hess said the approach benefits both fans and the business."There's no reason why every team in New York shouldn't do the same thing," he said.Emily DeVito, a senior adviser for economic policy at Groundwork Collaborative, also testified in Albany.She said New York has an

local.title: Western New York Heroes prepare to move into permanent home
local.summary: After nearly two decades of serving Western New York veterans, Western New York Heroes is preparing to move into a permanent home of its own, aided by an additional $1.8 million commitment that will help renovate the building.
local.body: After nearly two decades of serving Western New York veterans, Western New York Heroes is preparing to move into a permanent home of its own, aided by an additional $1.8 million commitment that will help renovate the building.The organization is moving into 235 North St. in Buffalo, ending years of renting and leasing space.“We can finally go from renting and years of leasing to a facility that is ours,” said Chris Kreiger, president and CEO of Western New York Heroes.WATCH: Western New York Heroes prepare to move into permanent homeNow in its 19th year, Western New York Heroes provides programs and services for local veterans. local.summary: The Men's Room Barbershop in Hamburg opened its chairs to veterans in honor of Veterans Day, offering free haircuts to anyone who served in the military.
local.body: For Gabrielle Genco, giving back to veterans hits close to home.Her husband, Donald, is a Marine Corps veteran who spent eight years in the infantry and completed two combat deployments. So when Gabrielle started thinking about how she could show her appreciation to those who served, she wanted to do something meaningful in her own community.Her idea was simple: free haircuts for veterans.Gabrielle brought the idea to her mother, Lori Notaro-Greene, who owns The Men's Room Barbershop in Hamburg. He says basic necessities can make a difference, particularly for veterans adjusting to civilian life after military service.Donald also emphasized the importance of veterans feeling comfortable seeking out support and services when they return home."Any veteran who comes home, sometimes there's a difficulty in adjustment, and I think the biggest thing is not being afraid to seek out services, even if it is a free haircut," he said.WATCH: Hamburg barbershop gives free haircuts to veterans in honor of Veterans DayThe effort also reflects the family's longstanding connection to the Hamburg community.Notaro-Greene has spent decades in the barbering business. local.title: Town of Hanover dedicates new Veterans Memorial on Veterans Day
local.summary: Hanover dedicated its new Veterans Memorial on Wednesday with a ceremony that also included the burial of a time capsule to be opened on July 4, 2076, the nation's 300th anniversary.
local.body: Hanover dedicated its new Veterans Memorial on Wednesday with a ceremony that also included the burial of a time capsule to be opened on July 4, 2076, the nation's 300th anniversary.Town Clerk Elizabeth VanCheri, who spearheaded the project, opened the ceremony by thanking attending veterans."This memorial was built for you," Hanover Town Clerk Elizabeth VanCheri said to those in attendance. Carter Knapp American Legion Post 953 of Forestville, recounted the history of Veterans Day.
